name: PT Telefast Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Telefast Indonesia: a voucher distributor priced as a platform
frontmatter.summary: We stay at SELL with a twelve-month target of Rp36, -74.6% from Rp140. The 2026 rebound is real but pass-through, the working-capital block is most of book value, and debt drawn against it ranks ahead of us. Every branch, the bull included, lands below the price.
thesis: This is a pass-through distributor, not a platform: gross margin is 3.3% and EBIT is IDR-0.8bn on revenue of IDR319.0bn, so revenue growth at that spread adds turnover, not value [S0].

The DCF is the primary lens at a 75% weight and gives Rp22 a share: an enterprise value of IDR82.9bn against net debt dated 30 June 2026 and minorities, with the debt drawn up by IDR6.1bn in the first half [S0].

Book value of 100.4 a share is not a floor. It sits mostly in stock and supplier advances, the price is 1.4x that book, and the report page lists annual reports only to the 2020 edition and their text is not archived [S0] [S24].
The EV/Sales cross-check uses the 0.31x that the distributor peers trade at, anchored on our own covered parent MCAS, and still gives only Rp45 a share [S0] [S11].
The asymmetry is in the tails: bear Rp13, base Rp32, bull Rp100 against a Rp140 price, so the risk is skew rather than timing [S0].

catalysts.event: Q3 2026 interim accounts were due; at this report date we hold no archived copy, so the release is the first hard test of the 1H26 rebound
IDX retires the E, D, A and S notation letters and starts the P notation for free-float shortfalls on the Accelerator board
FY2026 audited accounts due, the first audited set that could enter our archive since the FY2019 statements
The P notation reaches the Main and Development boards, where Telefast is listed, turning the float shortfall into a dated disclosure event

blocks.text: We keep PT Telefast Indonesia Tbk at **SELL** with a twelve-month target of **Rp36**, a total return of **-74.6%** from the Rp140 price. The market capitalisation is 233,225,482,000 rupiah on a free float of 13.0% and an average daily turnover of 189,836,240 rupiah, so the price is set by a thin float rather than by a contest over value [S0].

This revision changes the construction, not the direction. We cut the sales multiple from the platform-contaminated peer median to the distributor set that includes our own covered parent, set capital expenditure equal to depreciation so that property, plant and equipment stops going negative, modelled the debt the company drew in the first half of 2026 instead of holding it flat, and let the working-capital block unwind at half the pace the accounts show. The target falls, and the sales lens is now cut to a 25% weight so that the DCF, at 75%, supplies the larger part of the blend: Rp22 a share from the DCF against Rp45 from the sales multiple [S0]. The sales lens still supplies more rupiah per share than its weight implies, because its per-share value is 103.5% above the DCF; the weight, not the per-share output, is what we control.

The evidence base is weaker than the model. The FY2025 base year and the 1H26 anchor come from the vendor data pack [S0], not from a filing we can quote, and the financial-analysis section says exactly what we could and could not verify. We know the interim accounts exist at the exchange, because Telefast does not appear on either of the non-filer suspension lists we archived — neither the July list for the 31 March 2026 accounts nor the November continuation for the 30 June 2026 accounts [S28] [S29] — and a trailing loss per share of 12.99 rupiah from the market data is consistent with the pack's loss-making LTM [S6]. We have therefore kept the pack's lines, disclosed them, made no fact from a document we cannot quote, and cut the weight on the one method that leans hardest on the unverified revenue line.

The variant view is not that the company is failing. It is that the company is a distributor priced as a platform. Telefast resells operator vouchers and runs e-commerce drop points; its gross margin is 3.3% and its EBIT is IDR-0.8bn on revenue of IDR319.0bn [S0]. The 2026 recovery is real — revenue grows 49.0% in our forecast on a first half roughly half again as large as the year before [S0] — but it arrives at the same thin spread, so gross profit rises only to IDR12.0bn and EBIT to IDR0.5bn. Revenue growth in a pass-through business creates value only if the return on the capital it consumes clears the cost of capital, and the model says it does not.

Three things move the value: the spread, because a point of margin on this revenue base is worth more than the whole EBIT line; the working-capital block of IDR188.8bn, because it is most of book equity and we can decompose it only as far as the 2020 interim notes [S3]; and the debt, IDR40.5bn at the FY2025 balance sheet and higher at the 30 June 2026 date the valuation bridges from, which ranks ahead of the equity [S0].

Telefast was founded in 2008 as a telecommunications sales agent selling starter packs and vouchers to small phone shops, and it became an operator-appointed distributor for Banten and Central Java covering more than 10,000 retail stores [S22]. That distribution franchise — route sales to kiosks, warungs and phone counters — is still the backbone of the revenue line. In 2019 the company added human-resources services, and in 2020 it repositioned itself as a supply-chain business through its subsidiary PT Logitek Digital Nusantara, using drop points and a delivery network tied to the SiCepat express franchise [S22] [S20]. That description follows the company's own subsidiary page, which still lists Logitek as a subsidiary [S20]; an unarchived March 2025 press item suggested SiCepat and Onstar had sold Logitek and TFAS Energi to Skytron, and because we could not archive its text we neither remove the subsidiary nor book a disposal gain, and we flag the sale as an open item. The Fastpoint brand is the customer-facing piece of that logistics and fulfilment offer [S23].

The revenue mix follows from that history. The great majority of turnover is the resale of operator vouchers, data packages and digital products, where Telefast earns a distributor spread on goods it buys and resells almost immediately. The logistics and fulfilment line books delivery and handling revenue, again largely pass-through, and the human-resources line is small. This is why a company with revenue of IDR319.0bn reports cost of goods sold of IDR308.5bn and gross profit of only IDR10.5bn [S0]. The company has never published a segment note that we can source: the most recent audited accounts in our archive are the FY2019 statements, which present a single operating segment [S5].

The footprint is Java-centred, inherited from the original distributorship, and the network is the asset that matters — thousands of small counters that re-order daily. Telefast does not own the trucks or the warehouses in its logistics business in any meaningful way; capital expenditure ran at IDR0.1bn in FY2025 against depreciation of IDR1.3bn, and property, plant and equipment is a rounding error on the balance sheet [S0]. In a market of national distributors, large e-commerce platforms and thousands of sub-distributors, Telefast is a challenger with regional reach and no pricing power over either its suppliers or its retail customers.

Control sits with the digital-voucher group. At the time of the IPO the register showed PT M Cash Integrasi Tbk with 43.9%, PT Telefast Indonesia Investama Indonesia with 25.4%, PT Distribusi Voucher Nusantara Tbk with a further stake and the public with 16.7%, and the annual report describes MCAS, DVN and Telefast Investama as the controlling shareholders [S11]. The registry now shows insiders holding 71.1% and institutions 7.5%, with a free float of 13.0% [S0]. That structure explains both the company's access to voucher supply and its lack of independent bargaining position: its largest shareholder is also a principal in the same distribution chain, and the 2020 interim notes name MCAS as the immediate parent and Kresna Prima Invest as the ultimate parent [S3].

The voucher-distribution layer exists because prepaid phone credit and digital top-ups are sold mostly through small shops that cannot buy directly from the operators. A distributor buys bulk, holds a small float of stock, and sells in tiny denominations to thousands of counters, earning a percentage spread on each transaction while carrying credit risk and logistics cost. The spread is thin by construction, and it compresses as operators push users toward direct digital top-up and as e-commerce platforms bundle credit into their own checkout. Distributors survive on volume, working-capital discipline and route density rather than on brand or technology.

The addressable market is large and still growing. Indonesia had 235 million internet users in 2026, a penetration rate of 81.7%, according to the national survey reported in the press [S26]. The digital economy reached 102 billion US dollars of gross merchandise value in 2025, is projected at 119 billion in 2026 and 227 billion by 2030 [S27]. E-commerce alone accounted for about 71 billion US dollars in 2025 and is projected to keep growing at roughly 17.0% a year to 2035 [S25] [S27], while total digital GMV grew about 14.0% in 2025 [S25].

Telefast sits in the physical distribution and fulfilment layer beneath that GMV, not in the platform layer. Its revenue is a function of two things: the volume of prepaid credit and digital products that flows through small shops, and the parcels that move through its drop-point network. Both are growing in units and both are commoditising in price. The industry data describes a market expanding in value, but the share of that value captured by intermediaries is a separate question, and Telefast's own margin history is the evidence: the audited FY2019 accounts show gross profit of IDR55.0bn on revenue of IDR665.6bn [S5], while FY2022 gross margin was 5.4%, FY2023 5.9% and FY2025 3.3% [S0]. The market grew throughout that period; the spread did not, except for the FY2023 uptick that the next year gave back.

Five forces, in our reading, all point the same way. Supplier power is high: the operators and the large platforms set the wholesale price and can withdraw a product or change a commission schedule at will, and the group's own shareholders sit inside that supply chain [S11]. Buyer power is high and rising because a kiosk can switch distributor for a fraction of a rupiah per voucher and because consumers can top up directly through banking and e-wallet apps. The threat of substitution is structural rather than cyclical — every shift from a physical voucher to a direct digital top-up removes a transaction from the distribution layer. New entrants face low capital barriers, since a distributor needs stock and a route rather than a factory. Rivalry is intense among many regional distributors chasing the same counters, which is exactly the condition that compresses a spread.

Regulation matters in three ways, and this revision takes all three seriously. Disclosure first: an IDX-listed company must publish quarterly accounts and an annual report, and the exchange suspends issuers that do not — the July 2026 announcement covered 72 issuers missing the 31 March 2026 accounts and the November continuation covered the 30 June 2026 accounts, and Telefast appears on neither list [S28] [S29], so the filings exist even though we could not archive their text. Second, the trading regime: the exchange has retired the old E, D, A and S notation letters from 30 November 2026 and phased in a P notation for issuers that fall short of the minimum free-float requirement under Rule I-A, starting with the Accelerator board and reaching the Main and Development boards from 30 April 2027 [S30]. Third, the float itself: at 13.0% the registry float sits below that minimum, so the shortfall is a dated supply-or-dilution question rather than pure illiquidity [S0] [S30]. A suspended stock cannot be exited at any price, which is the reason the entry and exit assumptions in this note are stricter than the valuation alone would require.

We do not find a moat. There is no proprietary technology in the accounts, no long-term exclusive contract that we can source, and no scale advantage that shows up in the margin line: a company with scale advantage would not earn 3.3% on a pass-through product [S0]. The 10,000-store network is a real asset in the sense that it would cost money and years to replicate, but it is a distribution asset that the supplier can route around, and four years of margin data suggest the supplier has been doing exactly that [S5] [S0]. Our base case therefore does not credit the company with expanding its share of the value chain.

What we can and cannot verify. The FY2025 base year and the 1H26 anchor in this model are vendor data [S0]. We could not archive the FY2025 annual report, the FY2025 audited accounts or the 1H26 interim statements: the LK index lists statements to FY2023 [S2] and the report page lists annual reports to the 2020 edition [S24], but the text of neither page's documents is archived, and the FY2025 and FY2026 LK pages we tried returned an access error. We register no fact from a document we cannot quote. What we can say is that the statements exist, because the exchange's non-filer suspension lists for the 31 March 2026 and 30 June 2026 accounts do not include Telefast [S28] [S29]; that the trailing loss per share of 12.99 rupiah shown in the market data is consistent with a loss-making LTM [S6]; and that the last audited statements we hold are FY2019 [S5], and the only interims in the archive are 1Q20 and 1H20, both unaudited [S3] [S4], which supply the operating structure and the working-capital decomposition below. The practical consequence for the valuation is that we weight the lens most exposed to the unverified revenue line — EV/Sales — at 25% rather than as the primary method, and we say in the risk section that a data error in the vendor pack, not a misread of the business, is the main way this note could be wrong.

Revenue peaked at IDR765.5bn, then fell to IDR633.4bn, IDR401.9bn and IDR319.0bn in the three following years [S0]. Three consecutive years of contraction in a market that was growing is the single most important fact about this company: it lost share or lost products, and it did so while the industry expanded. The 2026 numbers break the pattern — revenue of IDR475.3bn in our forecast, growth of 49.0% — but the recovery is concentrated in a wholesale-like volume rebound rather than in a new product line, and it arrives at a lower spread than the business earned at the peak.

Gross margin tells the story of the model, and the direction matters: it was 5.4% in FY2022, rose to 5.9% in FY2023 — the best year in the available record — then fell to 3.4% and 3.3% [S0]. The first half of 2026 ran below the FY2025 average, and we model 2.5% for the full year before walking the spread to 3.3% by FY2030E, still far below the audited FY2019 margin of IDR55.0bn on IDR665.6bn [S5] and below the FY2022-FY2023 range, because those spreads came from a mix with more direct voucher sales that the pass-through volume of 2026 does not carry [S0]. Operating costs have been squeezed in response: SG&A was IDR18.5bn in FY2024 and IDR11.2bn in FY2025, and we hold the 1H26 ratio of 2.4% flat rather than shaving it further [S0]. Even so, EBIT was IDR-0.8bn in FY2025 and is IDR0.5bn in our forecast, a rounding error on IDR475.3bn of revenue. The operating leverage a distributor needs in order to be interesting is not there at this spread.

Below the operating line the accounts are messier than the business. FY2025 carried an interest charge of IDR6.6bn against interest income of IDR0.6bn, and a non-operating item of IDR-15.2bn that took profit before tax to IDR-22.0bn from an EBIT of IDR-0.8bn [S0]. We treat that charge as a one-off write-down and forecast none, but we cannot verify its nature without the FY2025 notes, which are not in our archive [S24]. The tax line is also unusable as a rate because it carries the opposite sign to the loss. One inconsistency remains unresolved: the reported net result of IDR-24.2bn is about the size of the non-operating charge, yet equity fell from IDR176.4bn to IDR167.1bn over the same year, a fall far smaller than the loss [S0]. Either a credit of roughly the charge's size moved through equity without appearing in the pack, or one of the two vendor figures is wrong. We take the loss as reported because it reconciles with the interest charge and the write-down, and we treat the book value as an upper bound — which cuts against the bull case, not for it.

Working capital is the balance-sheet issue, and this revision decomposes it. Non-cash working capital was IDR181.4bn, IDR211.4bn, IDR208.0bn and IDR188.8bn across the four years [S0] — it moved by less than a third while revenue fell by more than half. The archived notes tell us what is inside it: at 31 March 2020 inventories were IDR85.7bn and advances to suppliers IDR72.0bn, against trade receivables of IDR21.3bn [S3]. This is stock and supplier prepayment, not a receivable book, and describing the block as receivables and other current assets understates how much of it is physical or prepaid. Two readings are possible and they have opposite valuation consequences. Either the block is genuine, durable working capital that must be funded as revenue grows, in which case growth consumes cash; or part of it is impaired or slow-moving stock, in which case book equity of IDR167.1bn is overstated. Our model takes the middle path: it holds the block in absolute rupiah terms and lets it unwind by about the amount the last two years already show, half the observed pace, so that IDR160.0bn remains on the balance sheet at the end of the forecast rather than being released into the DCF as cash [S0] [S3].

Debt and cash are the second balance-sheet issue, and the direction changed in 2026. Gross debt fell from IDR69.0bn at the FY2024 balance sheet to IDR40.5bn a year later, but the company then drew IDR6.1bn in the first half of 2026, taking debt to IDR46.6bn at 30 June 2026 against cash of IDR2.3bn at the year end [S0]. The recovery is therefore debt-funded: we book the first-half drawdown in FY2026E and then amortise it as free cash flow allows, with debt down to IDR38.6bn by FY2030E and no new facilities. Net debt of IDR38.2bn was 78.8 times EBITDA — a meaningless multiple on an EBITDA of IDR0.5bn, but an accurate description of a company whose interest bill exceeds its operating profit. Operating cash flow was negative in both of the last two years, so the debt is serviced from the working-capital block rather than from earnings [S0]. The company has never paid a dividend and we forecast a payout of 0.0% throughout [S0] [S8].

Capital expenditure is the assumption we corrected most. Reported capex ran at IDR0.1bn in FY2025 and IDR1.1bn in our forecast, against depreciation of IDR1.3bn and IDR1.1bn [S0]. Keeping capex at the reported rate drove property, plant and equipment negative within two years, which is impossible, so we set capex equal to depreciation at 0.2% of revenue. Property, plant and equipment stays at IDR1.2bn through the forecast, and free cash flow to the firm is IDR13.3bn in FY2026, IDR5.3bn in FY2027 as the working-capital release slows, and IDR8.9bn in FY2030 [S0]. The network, drop points and delivery kit are largely partners' assets, but the company's own equipment still wears out and the maintenance spend has to be paid by someone.

Capital allocation has been passive. The only capital action in the record is the buyback mandate under which up to 9.8 m shares may be transferred out of the 2020 treasury holding and sold on the exchange at market prices through a broker [S9]; the figure is a ceiling, not an executed amount, and we do not know how much was placed. A buyback followed by a sell-down is not capital allocation; it is balance-sheet housekeeping that returns a small amount of stock to a thin market. There has been no rights issue, no acquisition we can source and no dividend.

On the earnings-quality screen we run before committing estimates: the accruals signal is negative but not decisive, because the loss is larger than the cash outflow — earnings are worse than cash, not better — and the gap is absorbed by the working-capital block [S0]. The divergence flag that matters is inventory and advances staying near their level while revenue halved: that is the signature of a stale asset or of a business that cannot collect as it shrinks, and it is why we keep the block on the balance sheet rather than release it. On the IDX regime flags the picture is better than the disclosure record suggests but not clean: Telefast is not on the exchange's non-filer suspension lists for the 2026 interim accounts [S28] [S29], and the P notation now being phased in is a free-float flag rather than a going-concern or late-filing flag [S30]. We could not verify whether the stock sits on the special-monitoring board: the Rule I-X regime that governs it is described in the notation article we hold [S30], but no archived source publishes the board's membership list, and absence from the suspension lists is not evidence of absence from that board, so we treat entry and exit as gated rather than assume either way. Related parties: sales to related parties were 0.8% of total sales in the last period we can quote, and purchases from the immediate parent MCAS were IDR0.1bn in that quarter against a small amount from NFC Indonesia [S3]; we cannot quantify the current-year flows, which is a gap we flag rather than fill. Structure flags: a treasury-share transfer mandate is in progress [S9], the free float is below the Rule I-A minimum [S0] [S30], and the last audited statements in our archive are FY2019 [S5]. We classify these as optics-class and information-class, not manipulation-class, and we allege no misconduct. We found no pledge disclosure in the archived filings; that is a statement about our archive, not a clearance.

A discounted cash flow is the right primary method here because the company's earnings are too thin for a P/E to mean anything and its book value is a working-capital block of unknown quality, while its cash flows are observable and its capital structure is simple. We use a five-year explicit forecast and a terminal value, with the horizon set in `params` rather than the ten-year default because the revenue line has already swung by more than half in three years and a longer line would be invention. The EV/Sales cross-check is the natural secondary lens: it is how the market actually prices distribution and platform-adjacent businesses in this sector, and it is the only multiple that survives a near-zero EBITDA.

Two lenses rather than the house's usual three is a deliberate choice, and the reason is in the accounts. A P/E cross-check is undefined because earnings per share are negative in the last reported year and negligible in our forecast; an EV/EBITDA cross-check produces a multiple in the hundreds, which prices nothing. The third candidate is P/BV, and we test it rather than dismiss it: at Rp100 of book value per share the stock trades at 1.4x book, and a peer P/BV would value the shares at more than the market price. We do not weight it, because a peer multiple on book value asserts that this particular book is recoverable at face value — and the book is precisely the asset we cannot verify. The asset case is therefore priced where it belongs, in the bull scenario; we would rather run two lenses we can defend than three where one is an assumption dressed as a multiple.

The cost of capital is 13.8%: a risk-free rate of 7.4%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2%, an Indonesian country risk premium of 2.5%, an unlevered beta of 1.20 that we have not shaded for the company's small size, and a re-levered beta of 1.39 at the observed debt-to-equity of 0.20. The cost of equity is 15.1%, and the discretionary premium on top of the measured betas is 0.0% — we add none — with the cost of debt 9.4% pre-tax, weighted 83.4% equity and 16.6% debt. The rupiah discount rate sits above the house's usual band because the betas and the country premium alone put it there; we have chosen not to add a small-cap premium on top, and the illiquidity of the stock is handled once, by the separate liquidity discount at the end, not twice.

The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR82.9bn and an equity value of Rp22 a share. Free cash flow to the firm is IDR13.3bn in FY2026 and IDR8.9bn in FY2030; the terminal value is 66.8% of the total, which is high but reflects a business whose explicit-period cash flow is tiny relative to any steady state. The bridge from enterprise value to equity is set out line by line in the DCF table: it deducts net debt and minorities dated 30 June 2026, not a forecast line. Net debt on that date is higher than the FY2025 year-end figure of IDR38.2bn by the IDR6.1bn the company drew in the first half [S0]. An earlier draft of this note used the FY2026E forecast net-debt line of IDR28.4bn as the bridge, which was wrong: a forecast line that assumes cash accumulates during the year cannot be subtracted from a valuation dated before that accumulation. The correction removes about a third of the equity value, and the resulting Rp22 a share is what the primary method actually says.

The EV/Sales cross-check gives Rp45 a share at 0.31 times sales, 103.5% above the DCF. The multiple is the crux of this revision, so here is the peer set in full. The industry screen returns six names with a sales multiple; we use three, and the table lists those three. PT M Cash Integrasi Tbk — MCAS, the 43.9% parent in the same voucher chain and a name this desk covers with a negative view [S11] — is the closest comparable because it shares the voucher-distribution model and the controlling shareholder. NFCX and EMTK are the other two distributors in the screen whose revenue comes from transaction and distribution volumes rather than from network ownership. We exclude KREN, which is a consumer-finance holding, BELI, which is a fixed-broadband platform, and WIFI, which is a network operator priced for infrastructure growth: none of the three trades on a distributor multiple, their sales multiples measure a different business, and using their median imports exactly the platform valuation this note argues against. The median of the three we keep lands on the parent's own multiple, so the sales lens no longer contradicts the DCF by an order of magnitude. We keep it at 25% because it captures the possibility that the network is bought for its reach, and because a single-method note would hide the one piece of evidence a buyer would use.

The blend, before the probability weighting and the illiquidity adjustment, is Rp28 a share. The twelve-month roll-forward at the cost of equity gives Rp32 for the base scenario, the probability-weighted average across the three scenarios is Rp44, and after the liquidity discount of 20.0% the target is Rp36 [S0]. The liquidity discount is the constitution's band for a stock with average daily turnover of 189,836,240 rupiah; it is not an analyst judgement and we do not adjust it.

The sensitivity table shows the target is most sensitive to the terminal spread and to the discount rate, and almost indifferent to capital expenditure because capex now equals depreciation rather than being free. A terminal growth rate at the top of the plausible range and a spread at the top of the FY2022 and FY2023 range together still do not close the gap to the market price, because the constraint is the spread times the revenue base, not the growth rate.

What the price implies. At Rp140 the market capitalisation is 233,225,482,000 rupiah, which is 1.4x our forecast book value and several times the IDR82.9bn enterprise value the DCF supports after net debt [S0]. The engine cannot bracket a reverse-DCF solution inside our assumption ranges, because EBIT is near zero and the growth or margin required to justify the price falls outside anything the company has earned since listing; we report that as the finding rather than force a number. Even the sales lens, at the multiple the parent trades at, values the shares below the price, so the market is paying for something — a platform, an acquisition, a relisting — that none of the three lenses can see.
The principal downside risks, with our likelihood and impact judgements:

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Why | |---|---|---|---| | Margin compression continues | High | High | The spread fell from the FY2023 peak to 3.3%, and the mix keeps shifting to pass-through volume [S0] | | Working-capital write-down or impairment | Medium | High | A block of IDR188.8bn sits in stock and supplier advances we cannot verify since the 2020 notes [S0] [S3] | | Liquidity, float and suspension | High | High | Free float 13.0%, turnover 189,836,240 rupiah, and a Rule I-A shortfall now flagged by the exchange [S0] [S30] | | Refinancing of debt | Medium | High | Interest of IDR6.6bn already exceeds EBIT, and debt rose again in the first half of 2026 [S0] | | Loss of a major supplier or platform contract | Medium | High | The controlling shareholder is in the same supply chain [S11] | | Reporting remains thin | Medium | Medium | No annual report text we hold after FY2019, though the interim filings are being made [S5] [S24] [S28] | | Related-party terms deteriorate | Medium | Medium | MCAS and DVN are both shareholder and counterparty [S11] [S3] |

The risk we weight most heavily is not any single line but the combination of a thin spread and a large, unverifiable asset base. A distributor with a durable spread can carry working capital; a distributor whose spread is compressed cannot, because the working capital is funded by debt that the spread no longer covers. That is also the way this note could be wrong about the business rather than about the numbers: if a third of the block is not real, the book value we treat as an upper bound is overstated and the bear case is too generous, not too harsh.

Our scenarios shock the same four drivers in mirrored steps — revenue growth, gross margin, the operating-cost ratio and working capital — and the shocks and their sizes are listed in the scenario table. The bear case takes 25% probability and values the shares at Rp13; the base takes 50% and gives Rp32; the bull takes 25% and gives Rp100. The distribution is wide — the bear sits more than a third below the base — because the DCF supplies most of the value and a levered, thin-margin cash flow is genuinely sensitive to volume and to the working-capital release. Revenue is shocked because it is not value-neutral: the engine's own sensitivity grid shows revenue growth and margin moving the target by comparable amounts, and the earlier draft's claim to the contrary was wrong.

The bear case is a stall in the 2026 rebound: a large voucher or drop-point counterparty is lost and revenue runs below our base, the mix goes fully pass-through and the spread compresses, the fixed cost base does not scale, and the working-capital block stops unwinding and starts absorbing cash as the stock ages. Inside that tail a distress branch is possible in which the block is written down far enough that the enterprise value falls toward the debt and the equity is worth close to nothing. We do not value it as a fourth scenario: the engine's three branches shock the same four drivers, and a write-down is a balance-sheet judgement rather than a driver shock, so a fourth branch would put an unmodelled probability on the target. We treat it as the qualitative floor beneath the bear instead, which is why we do not present book value a share as support. The base case is the recovery holding at today's spread with the block unwinding slowly and costs flat. The bull case is e-commerce GMV growth of roughly 17.0% a year feeding voucher and last-mile volumes, revenue above our base, the network re-signed at better spreads so the terminal gross margin reaches 5.4% — the FY2022 level, still below the FY2023 peak of 5.9% — and the stock and advances turning over faster, releasing cash rather than absorbing it. The bull is the asset case: it is what the shares are worth if the book is real and the spread returns to the best level of the last four years.

Signposts that would change our view: a gross margin above the FY2024 level for two consecutive quarters with revenue still growing; disclosure of the inventory and advances composition in an audited annual report; a debt reduction funded from operations rather than from working capital; a change in the controlling shareholder's economic interest, including a sale of the group's stake; confirmation of the unarchived 2025 report that Logitek and TFAS Energi were sold, which would change the asset base; and any tender offer at a premium to the traded price.

Ownership is concentrated and the controller is an operating counterparty. At the IPO, MCAS held 43.9%, Telefast Investama 25.4%, DVN a further stake, Sentra Rejeki a block and the public 16.7%, and the annual report names the first three as controlling shareholders [S11]; the 2020 interim notes name MCAS as the immediate parent [S3]. The registry now shows insiders at 71.1%, institutions at 7.5% and a free float of 13.0% [S0]. A float that small means the market price is a thin signal, it means any institutional position is effectively unbuildable at scale, and it is below the exchange's Rule I-A minimum — a shortfall the exchange will now flag with a P notation on this board from 30 April 2027 [S30]. We found no pledge disclosure in the archived filings; that is a statement about our archive, not a clearance.

Capital structure actions sit with the controller. The company holds treasury shares from a 2020 buyback and has a mandate to transfer up to 9.8 m shares out of that holding — a maximum, not an executed amount — into the market through a broker at prevailing prices [S9]. The effect is a supply overhang on a stock with a free float of 13.0%, and the timing sits with the controller rather than with minority holders. There has been no dividend in any year of the available record and none is proposed [S8].

Disclosure is the weakest part of the governance picture, and we separate what we know from what we cannot see. The LK index lists statements to FY2023 [S2] and the report page lists annual reports to the 2020 edition [S24], but the documents' text is not archived, so the FY2025 audited accounts and the 2026 interim statements are not in our archive. They are, however, being filed: Telefast is absent from both non-filer suspension lists we hold [S28] [S29]. The 2026 annual general meeting of 18 June 2026, whose materials we archived, approved the annual report, the auditor and remuneration and granted an investment mandate [S8] [S7]; that meeting pre-dates the 30 June 2026 balance sheet and is context, not a post-balance-sheet event. We have not seen the auditor's opinion for any year after FY2019, whose accounts were audited and unqualified [S5]. Since the 30 June 2026 balance-sheet date we searched the exchange's suspension announcements of 30 July 2026 and 5 November 2026 [S28] [S29], the treasury-transfer notices through 2025 [S9], and Indonesian market press to 14 November 2026; we found no dividend, rights issue, acquisition, divestment or tender offer in that window, and we could not archive the interim LK itself, which is the gap the financial-analysis section discloses.

On ESG, the exposures are the ones that come with the business rather than with a factory. Labour standards in the drop-point and delivery network are the main social risk, because the last-mile partners are franchisees and the company's control over their employment practices is indirect [S22]. Data privacy matters in the human-resources services line, which handles candidate data, and in any customer data held at the drop points. Environmental exposure is limited by the asset-light model — no smelting, no mining, no large fuel burn on the company's own books — but the logistics network's emissions are real and outside the reported boundary. None of these is a valuation driver today; they are disclosure gaps we would want closed before taking a long position.

The dated catalysts are the reporting cycle, because each release is an information event for a stock with this little disclosure. The Q3 2026 interim accounts were due on 31 October 2026 and were not in our archive at the report date [S2]; they are the first hard test of the 1H26 rebound. The FY2026 audited accounts, due by the end of the first quarter of 2027, would be the first full audited set that could enter our archive since the FY2019 statements [S5] and the first chance to see the notes behind the IDR188.8bn working-capital block [S24]. On the exchange calendar, the E, D, A and S notation letters are retired from 30 November 2026 and the P notation for free-float shortfalls reaches this board from 30 April 2027 [S30]; the treasury-transfer mandate is a residual supply question [S9]; and the annual digital-economy GMV update gives the demand backdrop for voucher and parcel volumes [S27].

Between updates we watch five numbers: gross margin, which is the whole investment case; revenue growth against the 14.0% we model for FY2027; the absolute level of non-cash working capital against the IDR176.0bn in our forecast; gross debt against the IDR46.6bn we assume at the 2026 year end; and, as a data check on this note rather than on the company, any published revenue close to our FY2026E IDR475.3bn. If the first turns up and the third turns down, the thesis changes and we will say so. Until then the evidence supports SELL at a target of Rp36 [S0].

bear.narrative: The 2026 rebound reverses: a large voucher or drop-point counterparty is lost and revenue runs a fifth below our base, the spread goes to 0.5% as the mix turns fully pass-through, the fixed cost base does not scale, and the working-capital block stops unwinding and starts absorbing cash again as the stock ages - the impairment case, in which the block is worth less than the balance sheet says and book equity overstates the collateral behind the debt.

bull.narrative: The recovery holds and then some: e-commerce GMV growth of about 17% a year feeds voucher and last-mile volume, revenue runs a fifth above our base, the network is re-signed at better spreads so gross margin returns to 5.3% by FY2030E - essentially the FY2022 level and still below the FY2023 peak - and the stock and advances turn over faster, releasing cash rather than absorbing it.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +49% follows the first-half 2026 run-rate: revenue of Rp233.4bn in 1H26 against Rp156.8bn in 1H25, with Q2 2026 at Rp123.6bn versus Rp73.5bn a year earlier. Growth then fades toward the digital-economy trend: e-Conomy SEA puts Indonesian e-commerce GMV growth at about 17% a year to 2035 and total digital GMV at US$119bn in 2026 from US$102bn in 2025. A voucher/logistics distributor takes a thin cut of that GMV, so we fade to 8% by FY2030E and 5% in the long run rather than holding the underlying GMV rate.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: We start at the 1H26 actual (gross profit Rp5.81bn on Rp233.4bn) and walk the spread back to the last audited-year level of 3.28% (FY2025) by FY2030E as the fixed part of the buying and drop-point cost is spread over a larger top line. We do not go above the last annual actual: the 5.39-5.92% of FY2022-23 came from a mix with more direct voucher sales that the 2026 pass-through logistics volume does not carry.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating costs were 2.41% of revenue in 1H26 against 3.53% in FY2025 and 4.61% in FY2024: the rupiah cost base is largely fixed and the revenue recovery has already done the operating leverage. We hold the 1H26 ratio flat rather than shaving it further - no cost assumption beyond the last actual.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Depreciation and amortisation were 0.23% of revenue in 1H26 and 0.40% in FY2025 on a small fixed-asset base (PPE Rp1.06bn at 30 June 2026); we hold 0.23% with no step-up because capex stays minimal.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Capex must at least replace depreciation or property, plant and equipment goes negative, which is impossible. Reported capex ran at 0.03-0.06% of revenue (Rp0.10bn in FY2025, Rp0.14bn in 1H26) while depreciation ran at 0.23%, so we set capex equal to D&A: the network, drop points and delivery kit are partners' assets, but the company's own equipment still wears out.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: The block is stock and supplier advances, not receivables: at 31 March 2020 inventories were Rp85.7bn and advances Rp72.0bn against trade receivables of Rp21.3bn [S3]. It fell from Rp211.4bn (FY2023) to Rp188.8bn (FY2025) and Rp181.2bn at 30 June 2026 while revenue halved, so it is already unwinding. We continue that unwind at about Rp5bn a year - half the observed pace - rather than holding it rigidly or resetting it as a pure percentage of revenue; the ratio therefore falls as revenue grows.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Statutory Indonesian corporate rate of 22%; the company has tax losses carried forward, so the modelled charge only bites once EBIT turns positive. The reported FY2025 and FY2024 tax lines carry opposite signs on losses and are not a usable effective rate.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Interest expense of Rp6.60bn in FY2025 on opening debt of Rp69.0bn is 9.6%, and 1H26 interest of Rp1.95bn on about Rp45bn of debt is roughly 8.5% annualised; we use 9.0% against the bank-loan and working-capital facilities the company rolls over.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Cash balances are tiny (Rp2.32bn at 30 June 2026) and earn near-nothing; 2% is a conservative money-market yield on the opening balance.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: The 30 June 2026 balance sheet shows debt of Rp46.6bn against Rp40.5bn at the FY2025 year end, so Rp6.1bn was drawn in the first half; we book that drawdown in FY2026E and then assume Rp2bn a year of amortisation out of free cash flow, in line with the Rp28.5bn paydown recorded in FY2025. No new facilities and no refinancing need.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2025 carried a Rp-15.2bn non-operating charge outside EBIT and net interest (the reported PBT of Rp-22.0bn against EBIT of Rp-0.8bn and net interest of Rp-6.0bn). We treat it as a one-off write-down and forecast no repeat.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority interest in the balance sheet is Rp1.71bn against equity of Rp166.7bn, and the minority share of profit has been within Rp0.2bn of zero; we hold 1%.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend has been paid in any year of the available history and the company is loss-making with negative operating cash flow (Rp-6.2bn in FY2025, Rp-7.7bn LTM); we assume no dividend over the forecast.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Shares outstanding have moved only from 1,656.8m to 1,665.9m since FY2022 (employee share plans). No rights issue is in the 2026 meeting agenda, which covers only the annual report, the auditor and remuneration plus an investment mandate.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4% in rupiah is below Indonesian long-run nominal GDP growth and well below the 17% e-commerce GMV growth the industry report projects; a thin-margin distributor does not deserve the industry rate in perpetuity.

challenges.challenge: The FY2025 base year and the 1H26 anchor are vendor data, not filings: fund record holds no post-2019 P&L or balance-sheet fact, every FY2025/1H26 figure (revenue 318.97 and 233.4, gross profit 5.81, debt 46.6, cash 2.32, NWC 181.2) is cited only to Yahoo [S0], and section 6 itself states the FY2025 audited accounts and the 2026 interim statements are not published in the archive. The LTM revenue of 395.7 that drives 97% of the target (0.4 x Rp104.5 of Rp42.9) is derived from three unverified numbers: 318.97 - 156.8 + 233.4.
challenges.answer: The evidence base is now disclosed at the top of the summary and in section 3: the FY2025 base year and 1H26 anchor are vendor data [S0]. We could not archive either LK - the IR index stops at the FY2023 annual report [S24] and the LK pages returned an access error - so we make no fact from them and quote nothing we cannot verify. We proved the filings exist instead: TFAS is absent from BEI's non-filer suspension lists for both the 31 March 2026 and 30 June 2026 accounts [S28] [S29], and the trailing loss per share of 12.99 corroborates the LTM loss [S6]. EV/Sales weight cut to 40% and its multiple cut to the distributor median, so the unverified revenue no longer drives the target.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says the bridge uses 'net debt of about 32.4' and that 32.4 and minorities of 1.8 'come off an enterprise value of 49.1, leaving almost nothing'. That arithmetic leaves Rp14.9bn (Rp8.9/share), not Rp2, and it contradicts the engine bridge of 44.25 (debt 46.58 less cash 2.32 at 30 June 2026) and the QC justification's own 46.6. The report's FY2026E net-debt line of 32.45 is a forecast line, not the valuation-date bridge.
challenges.answer: Correct: the FY2026E net-debt line was a forecast and the bridge now uses the 30 June 2026 balance sheet. The engine's DCF bridge deducts net debt 44.25 and minorities 1.71 from an enterprise value of 82.87, giving equity of 36.9 (Rp22/share); the report points to the DCF table for the line items and explains in prose that 30 June net debt is higher than the FY2025 year-end figure of 38.2 by the 6.1 drawn in the first half [S0]. The 32.4 number is gone from the report.

challenges.challenge: The DCF is called primary but supplies 2.6% of the target: 0.4 x Rp104.5 EV/Sales = Rp41.8 of the Rp42.9 pre-discount blend, against 0.6 x Rp1.87 = Rp1.1 for the DCF. The note concedes peer revenue 'carries a different mix' yet keeps the 0.5561x peer median at 40% because dropping it 'would look like we had chosen the answer'. The closest comparable is MCAS, the 43.9% parent in the same voucher chain, at 0.306x EV/Sales (house-covered, SELL); at 0.31x the lens gives Rp45/share and the blended target falls to about Rp25, a -82% return.
challenges.answer: All six peers are named in section 4 and shown in the peer table: KREN (consumer-finance holding), BELI (fixed-broadband platform) and WIFI (network operator) are excluded with reasons; the set is MCAS, NFCX and EMTK, which gives 0.306x, identical to MCAS's own multiple [S0] [S11]. Weight stays 40% but with the corrected multiple the lens gives Rp45/share instead of Rp104.5, and the DCF is now the primary method at 60%.

challenges.challenge: The bear case is not a bear case: the shocks are only gross margin -0.6pp and opex +0.6pp, the EV/Sales lens carrying 97% of value is untouched, and the bear lands at Rp48 against a base of Rp49. The bear narrative (loss of another large counterparty, a fresh inventory write-down) contains no revenue shock and no write-down shock. A going-concern case is never valued even though debt is 46.6 against cash 2.3 and interest of 6.6 already exceeds EBIT; the 40% EV/Sales weight instead imposes a floor near Rp33 on a company the DCF values at Rp2.
challenges.answer: The bear now shocks four drivers in mirrored steps: revenue growth x0.8, gross margin -2pp, opex +1pp and working capital x1.1. It values the shares at Rp21 against a base of Rp36, and the narrative carries the inventory/advance write-down and an explicit zero-equity distress branch inside the bear, which we judge the more likely part of that tail because the asset behind the debt is unverified [S3].

challenges.challenge: Section 5 justifies not shocking revenue because growth is 'value-neutral at the current spread', but the model's own 12-month tp sensitivity grid shows revenue growth +4pp every year lifting the value from Rp49.4 to Rp92.2 (+87%), the same as gross margin +2pp; only the downside is flat because the DCF is floored. Section 5 also states probabilities of 0.2 bear, 0.5 base and 0.2 bull (sum 0.9) while the model uses 0.25/0.50/0.25 and the target is 0.8 x 55.5.
challenges.answer: The value-neutral claim is deleted and replaced with the engine's own finding that revenue growth and margin move the value by comparable amounts. The probabilities in the prose now read the model's 25/50/25 via the pct0 placeholder, so section 5 and the scenario engine agree; the earlier 0.2/0.5/0.2 text is gone.

challenges.challenge: The asset case is never stated. Equity of Rp166.7bn on 1,665.9m shares is BVPS Rp100; at Rp140 the stock is 1.4x book and 0.7x LTM sales. The report dismisses P/B as 'circular' and never gives BVPS or a recoverable range for the 181bn block it calls its key uncertainty. The archive does decompose it: S3 (31 March 2020) shows inventory Rp85.7bn and advances Rp72.0bn against trade receivables of Rp22.2bn, and audited FY2019 [S5] shows inventory Rp78.3bn and advances Rp41.6bn - stock and supplier prepayments, not the 'receivables, inventory and other current assets' of the summary. If half is realisable the asset value alone exceeds the target.
challenges.answer: BVPS of Rp100.4 and the 1.4x book at the Rp140 price are now stated, and the block is decomposed from the archived notes: inventory 85.7 and supplier advances 72.0 against trade receivables of 21.3 at 31 March 2020 [S3]. The recoverable-value case is the bull and the impairment case is in the bear. We still do not weight a peer P/BV - it would assert the book is recoverable at face value, which is the open question - and section 4 says so explicitly.

challenges.challenge: The bull refuses a margin the company earned two years ago. FY2023 gross margin was 5.92% (37.49/633.4) and FY2022 5.39%; the bull adds only 0.6pp to 3.1%, giving an EBIT margin near 1.3% against FY2019's 4.4%, yet its narrative claims 'operating margin reaches the best level the company has ever recorded' and section 5 says explicitly that the bull does not get the FY2019 margin. No scenario tests a return to the FY2023 spread that is in the model's own history.
challenges.answer: The bull now adds two points of gross margin to the base path, ending near the FY2022 spread of 5.4% and still below the FY2023 peak of 5.9% [S0]; the narrative was rewritten to match exactly that, and no longer claims a best-ever operating margin or denies the company's own FY2022/FY2023 history.

challenges.challenge: Regulatory and disclosure risk is underweighted. The FY2025 annual report (due 30 June 2026) and the 2Q26 LK are unpublished, and section 7 says Q3 2026 is 'due in the fourth quarter of 2026' when its IDX deadline was 31 October 2026, so it is overdue at the report date; late filing brings a written warning and then suspension, and a suspended stock cannot be exited, which changes the entry/exit assumptions in section 2. The claim 'we found no notation flag in the registry data we hold [S0]' is not evidence, because Yahoo does not carry IDX board or notation status. The registry also shows free float 12.97% against the new 15% minimum (non-compliant, deadline 31 March 2029), treated only as illiquidity rather than as future supply of about 34m shares.
challenges.answer: Regulatory risk is now sourced and dated: TFAS is absent from BEI's 30 July 2026 list of 72 issuers missing the 31 March 2026 accounts and from the 5 November 2026 continuation covering the 30 June 2026 accounts [S28] [S29], so late filing is not the live risk; the free-float shortfall is, and the P notation for Rule I-A shortfalls reaches the Main board from 30 April 2027 [S30]. The Q3 2026 deadline is corrected to 31 October 2026 and the float is treated as a dated supply-or-dilution event, not mere illiquidity.

challenges.challenge: Capex of 0.03-0.05% of revenue against D&A of 0.23% drives PPE negative in the model (FY2027 -0.73, FY2030 -4.52), which is impossible: sustaining capex of about Rp1.1bn a year is uncosted. Adding it cuts FCFF by roughly Rp0.9bn a year and Rp5-6 per share of value, which removes the DCF's entire Rp1.87 equity value. Separately, debt is held flat at 40.5 while the 30 June 2026 balance sheet shows 46.58 (up 6.1bn in 1H26) and the model books 5.7bn of cash accumulation instead - the recovery has been debt-funded.
challenges.answer: Capex is set equal to D&A at 0.23% of revenue, so property, plant and equipment stays at 1.2 through FY2030 and never goes negative. The 1H26 debt movement is modelled: net borrowing of +6.075 in FY2026E then amortisation, with gross debt falling to 38.6 by FY2030E, instead of a flat debt line with cash accumulating [S0]. Both changes are disclosed in section 3 as corrections to the draft.

challenges.challenge: The report asserts 'no related-party revenue flow we can quantify from the available filings' and that 'the transaction amounts are not in our archive', and gives no related-party percentage of revenue, which the earnings-quality card requires. S3 in the archive (Q1 2020 interim, note 9d) quantifies related-party sales of Rp1.226bn in Q1 2020 and Rp0.752bn in Q1 2019 (about 0.8% of quarterly revenue) and related-party purchases including MCAS Rp72.3m and NFC Rp15.4m; S3 page 11 names PT M Cash Integrasi as the immediate parent and Kresna Prima Invest as the ultimate parent.
challenges.answer: Note 9d is now cited: related-party sales were 0.84% of total sales in Q1 2020 (0.56% a year earlier) and purchases from MCAS were Rp72.3m with Rp15.4m from NFC Indonesia [S3]. The 'not in our archive' statement was wrong and is removed; the report also names MCAS as immediate parent and Kresna Prima Invest as ultimate parent from page 11 of the same filing.

challenges.challenge: Several verifiable errors: the post-balance-sheet review cites the 18 June 2026 AGM and the 29 October-31 December 2025 treasury sell-down, both before the 30 June 2026 balance-sheet date, so no event after it has been examined; section 6 renders '9.8 m shares million shares' and F9's quote is 'Sebanyak-banyaknya 9.849.600' (a maximum mandate, not the executed amount); section 3 says gross margin 'fell to 5.9%' in FY2023 when it rose from 5.39% to 5.92%, and section 5's 'fallen every year since the FY2019 audited peak' is therefore false; section 7 monitors FY2027 growth 'against the 0.1 we model' when the model is 14.0%; and the FY2025 net loss of 24.06 is 2.6x the 9.2 fall in equity, which the report flags but does not resolve while using both.
challenges.answer: Fixed: the 9.8m-share line now reads as a transfer mandate with its real unit [S9]; the post-balance-sheet search lists BEI's 30 July 2026 and 5 November 2026 announcements plus press to 14 November 2026 [S28] [S29]; the margin trend is corrected to a rise to 5.9% in FY2023 before the fall; section 7 monitors growth against the 14.0% we model; and the FY2025 loss of 24.2 against a 9.3 fall in equity is now stated as an unresolved inconsistency, with book value treated as an upper bound.

missing_bull_case.note: Asset backing (BVPS Rp100, 1.4x book, 0.7x sales) and a return to the FY2023 5.92% gross margin are never valued; the bull is capped at +0.6pp and its narrative claims a best-ever margin the shocks do not deliver.

missing_bear_case.note: No credible downside: the bear lands 2% below base, revenue and the EV/Sales multiple are not shocked, there is no write-down and no going-concern or zero-equity case, and suspension and free-float risk are treated as information risk only.

assumption_realism.note: Capex below D&A drives PPE negative (-0.73 in FY2027, -4.52 in FY2030), debt is held flat at 40.5 after the 30 June 2026 actual of 46.6, and the FY2025/1H26 base inputs are vendor data; terminal gross margin 3.0% and opex 2.28% both sit below the last actuals.

evidence_and_citations.note: The dominant LTM revenue of 395.7 and every post-2019 financial figure come from Yahoo [S0] with no fact record while section 6 says the statements are unpublished; the related-party assertion is contradicted by S3 note 9d, and the post-balance-sheet review dates precede the 30 June 2026 balance-sheet date.

valuation_method_fit.note: 97% of the pre-discount value is the EV/Sales lens the note says does not apply (sibling MCAS trades at 0.31x against the 0.5561x median used); the prose bridge uses net debt 32.4 instead of the engine's 44.3, and the 40% weight is justified by appearance rather than evidence.

bias_and_tone.note: Section 5 gives probabilities 0.2/0.5/0.2 against the model's 0.25/0.50/0.25; the claim that revenue is value-neutral is contradicted by the model's own tp sensitivity (+87% at +4pp growth); the target is 24x the primary method's own output.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The name is entirely IDR with no royalty, benchmark or realisation variable to read from the decks; terminal growth of 4.0% sits below the deck's CPI of 3.28% plus real growth, and the rate-sensitive AVOID tilt is consistent with the note. No deck contradiction found.

conservatism_audit.note: Downward drift beyond the last actual: terminal gross margin 3.0% vs FY2025 3.28% and FY2023 5.92%; opex 2.28% vs 1H26 2.41%; the 181bn working-capital block is never released; and an above-band COE of 15.1% plus a 20% liquidity discount price illiquidity twice. Conversely, capex below D&A and a flat debt line are unjustified optimism.

calibration.note: The gate passes only because FY2025 actual and model EBITDA margins are both near zero (0.15% vs 0.35%, a 0.20pp gap), so it proves nothing; the real FY+1 test, revenue +49% with gross margin -76bp, rests on the unverified 1H26 vendor data.

signoff.notes: Publishable as the house view. All FATAL/MATERIAL challenges C1-C11 are answered on substance: the bridge now deducts 30 June 2026 net debt 44.25 and minorities 1.71 from EV 82.9 (DCF equity 36.9 -> Rp22/share) rather than the forecast line; the bear and bull mirror the same four drivers (revenue growth x0.8/x1.2, gross margin -/+2pp, opex -/+0.5pp, NWC x1.1/x0.9) at 25/50/25 with base 50%; capex is set equal to D&A so PPE stays at 1.2 and never goes negative; the related-party flows (0.84% of Q1 2020 sales, MCAS purchases Rp72.3m, NFC Rp15.4m) are cited from note 9d; and the post-balance-sheet search is properly dated (BEI 30 Jul and 5 Nov 2026 lists, both of which TFAS is verifiably absent from). The evidence gap is handled honestly and prominently: the FY2025 base year and 1H26 anchor are vendor data [S0], no fact is registered from an unquotable document, the FY2025/1H26 LK text and post-1H20 filings are declared unarchived, and the unresolved equity-vs-loss reconciliation (176.4 -> 167.1 against a Rp24.2bn reported loss) is disclosed rather than smoothed. The base path follows the most-likely method: FY2026E +49.0% reproduces the 1H26 run-rate (233.4 vs 156.8), gross margin starts at the 1H26 actual 2.49% and walks only to the FY2025 actual 3.28%, opex held at the 1H26 2.41%, and the only haircut is the disclosed house liquidity band (20%, constitution ADTV rule). Batch bias check: no shared cause; peers are mixed (BUKA/GOTO/WIFI BUY, BELI REDUCE, NFCX SELL), TFAS WACC 13.82% and g 4.0% sit inside the peer range, and the SELL is company-specific (thin spread, debt-funded recovery, unverifiable Rp188.8bn working-capital block). The call is robust: even the bull case Rp100.48 is 28% below the Rp140 price, and the house default 60/40 weights give Rp37, still -73%. Q1-Q6 remain non-blocking NOTEs; for the record, Q2 (bull terminal margin prose 5.4% vs model 5.3%), Q5 (the rationale cutting the weight on the lens hardest on the unverified revenue line is repeated in the summary and section 3 and is weak, though the weight change does not move the rating) and Q4 (FY2026E net-debt line about 2.6bn low, outside the valuation) should be tidied at the next refresh. No consensus or broker material encountered. Approved for publication.

bias.note: Base case is anchored to the last actual, not stacked either way: FY2026E revenue +49% reproduces the 1H26 run-rate (233.4 vs 156.8) [S0]; gross margin starts at the 1H26 actual 2.49% and walks only to the FY2025 actual 3.28% [S0]; opex held at the 1H26 2.41%; capex set equal to D&A 0.23% fixes the negative-PPE defect; royalty n/a. The fade to 8% growth and 4% terminal is below the cited 17% GMV rate [S27] and is a mild unsourced conservatism, but it is argued from the distributor spread and partly offset by the bridge using a six-month-later net debt (44.25 vs 38.18 at FY2025A), which is conservative. Scenarios are mirrored on the same four drivers (revenue x0.8/x1.2, GM -/+2pp, opex -/+0.5pp, NWC x1.1/x0.9) and base is 50% >= 40%. Weights 75/25 are argued. No directional skew that moves the rating; the SELL survives even the bull case.

Third, book equity of Rp167.1bn is mostly stock and supplier advances whose recoverability we cannot check: the last audited statements in our archive are FY2019 [S5], the only interims are 1Q20 and 1H20 [S3] [S4], and the last annual report whose text we have archived is not later than the 2020 edition [S24]; the FY2025 report was approved at the 18 June 2026 AGM [S8] but could not be archived.
